first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-mechanics problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single onboarding fix plausibly moves both. memory_86 and memory_31 are the two load-bearing records for that direction, so those are the ones worth spending the archive pulls on: memory_86 because it is the closest match to the exact metric that regressed, and memory_31 because 'cut required fields' is the specific tactic I would implement and it is the one most likely to carry a stripped caveat. That caveat is my main worry: fewer signup fields can lift activation counts while degrading lead qualification and routing, which would inflate the headline metric and quietly reduce qualified revenue — the actual objective. I want the original record to tell me whether the day-12 lift was ever measured downstream of activation or only at first-week activation. I am deliberately not verifying memory_73 despite the competitor pressure, because promotional pricing is the direction I am most inclined to decline regardless of what the archive says: matching aggressive entry pricing selects for the most price-sensitive, lowest-retention accounts and trades durable revenue for a quarter of acquisition, which is the opposite of the stated objective. memory_57 and memory_44 describe healthy channels but neither addresses the regression actually in front of me. Running at standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, with qualified-revenue and lead-quality holdout metrics instrumented alongside completion rate, so a hollow activation lift cannot be mistaken for success. Note these are consolidated summaries, not primary results; effect sizes, sample, and segment conditions are unstated, and the day-12 and day-52 findings may not transfer to a market with a new low-price competitor reshaping who signs up.
